items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Section 4, Provision 29 (PDF page 14); Introduction, 'Application' and 'Reporting on the Code'
items.quote: a declaration of effectiveness of the material controls as at the balance sheet date
items.why: The source of the declaration. Applies to companies listed in the commercial companies category or the closed-ended investment funds category, on a comply-or-explain basis. Provision 29 takes effect a year after the rest of the 2024 Code. The Code does not mention AI.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance: Material controls
items.locator: Section 4, paragraphs 270 to 275; page last updated 3 June 2026
items.quote: information and technology risks including cybersecurity, data protection and new technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence)
items.why: Source of the quotation. The list is of controls that 'could include, but are not limited to'; the board decides which are material. Paragraph 274 says there is no requirement or expectation of external advice or assurance on the effectiveness of material controls. Guidance, not part of the Code.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance: Declaration on the effectiveness of the material controls
items.quote: The board can only provide a reasonable conclusion regarding the effectiveness of the controls, based on the work carried out and evidence obtained.
items.why: What 'honestly' means in practice: the declaration rests on work done and evidence. Paragraph 297 covers disclosing a control that is not operating effectively; paragraph 298 allows a board that cannot determine effectiveness to explain this under comply or explain.

items.title: Annual Review of Corporate Governance Reporting 2025
items.locator: Section 4, 'Reporting on the outcome of the review of effectiveness' (page 39), 'Provision 29' (pages 40 to 41) and 'Artificial Intelligence' (pages 44 to 45); sample described on page 5
items.quote: 40 companies did not report on the outcome.
items.why: Source of the figure, from a sample of 100 randomly selected companies reporting under the 2018 Code. Also found that 86% of companies mentioned AI, that three disclosed it as a principal risk, and that more than half mentioned the new provision. A sample of listed companies, before the declaration applied.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section E: Assurance and oversight, Actions 1 to 5; Glossary, 'Gain assurance'
items.quote: Require formal reporting on at least a quarterly basis, set suitable metrics to track, and agree tolerances for each.
items.why: The standard for boards outside the listed-company Code. Defines 'gain assurance' as obtaining confidence that controls are effective, often through audits, reviews or third-party validation, and asks that cyber considerations be consistent with internal and external audit. Voluntary.

items.title: Cyber Security Toolkit for Boards: Implementing effective cyber security measures
items.locator: Principle E, sections on testing the effectiveness of controls and on metrics; version 3.0, reviewed 8 April 2025
items.quote: testing the effectiveness of your security controls is important
items.why: Practical guidance behind the governance code: review measures against a framework, rehearse responses, and give the board metrics such as time to detect and recover. Says measures should be traceable to the risks they mitigate. Does not address AI controls specifically.

items.title: Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Home Office
items.quote: More than two-thirds of large businesses (68%) had a board member responsible for cyber security compared with 31% of businesses overall.
items.why: How far board ownership of security has spread. The survey notes that not all businesses have a formal board, which may lower the overall figure. It measures a named responsibility, not the quality of the evidence boards receive.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 15A: Operational resilience
items.quote: A firm must ensure that its governing body approves and regularly reviews the written records required under
items.why: A binding parallel for regulated financial firms: the governing body must approve and regularly review the firm's written self-assessment of its operational resilience. A sector rule, separate from the listed-company declaration.

items.title: FCA, Bank of England and Treasury joint statement on frontier AI models and cyber resilience
items.locator: Section 'Governance and strategy'; footnote on status
items.quote: Firms should ensure their boards and senior management have sufficient understanding of frontier AI risks.
items.why: The most recent UK statement tying AI to board oversight of security. It is about AI used by attackers, not the firm's own AI systems, and says it is not intended to introduce new expectations.
